doc.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017

chapter: Henderson, Goodman and the swing era
title: Benny Carter insists on being paid in cash
summary: Gentlemen like Carter and Hinton would defend their professionalism; Carter demanded cash from a club owner.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Wow. You know what I loved about Joe and I noticed it with Milt Hinton and other fellows of that generation is they were such gentlemen, they were so nice, but at the same time if you disrespected them, like in a business fashion or — I witnessed this like a couple of times. Someone suggesting that they weren’t living up to their obligations. They took the heat and they were wait a minute, don’t besmirch my professionalism. And it was really good to witness that. You can be a nice guy and also stand up for your —

I saw it with Benny Carter also. He played a club in New York, Carlos #1 I guess it was. It was a club that was on Sixth Avenue. And he insisted on being paid in cash. And the guy said he would, the owner of the club said he would. And the guy was going to go back on that after Benny had played. And Benny insisted, “You give me my cash, this is what we agreed on — you don’t give me my cash you know —.” I don’t know what the consequences would have been but it was quite obvious that he was making Benny very angry. And you don’t get Benny Carter angry. That’s a side of Benny you don’t want to see.

Yeah. All that stuff about him being a gentleman and all that stuff. Yeah, he is, but don’t rile him. Don’t mess with him. Really. He got his cash. Believe me. At the end of the night he got his cash. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
